You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: AMD: $1 Trillion Market Cap Marks the Shift Toward Full-Stack AI Systems

TEXT:
Beyond $1 Trillion, the Market Is Repricing AMD
AMD surged nearly 10% on September 21, closing around $615.5 at a record high and pushing its market capitalization above $1 trillion for the first time. The stock has gained roughly 185% in 2026, significantly outperforming the Nasdaq. The rally also came amid renewed strength across the semiconductor sector, with names such as Intel and Arm rising sharply as capital rotated back into AI and compute-related stocks.
The bigger story is that AMD is no longer being valued simply as “the company chasing NVIDIA .” Its business positioning is evolving from a CPU and GPU supplier into a broader AI infrastructure platform spanning GPUs, EPYC CPUs, networking, ROCm software, and rack-scale systems. The Helios rack-scale architecture unveiled in July integrates 72 MI455X GPUs with 18 sixth-generation EPYC processors. OpenAI is expected to begin deployments in the fourth quarter of 2026, while Meta , Anthropic , Microsoft and other major customers are also moving into validation or broader deployment phases.
Data Center Has Become the Core Growth Engine
AMD reported second-quarter revenue of $11.5 billion, up 50% year over year. Data Center revenue reached $6.7 billion, up 107%, accounting for close to 60% of total revenue. Non-GAAP EPS rose 246% to $1.66, while non-GAAP operating margin expanded to 27%. Growth was driven by both EPYC server CPUs and Instinct GPUs, showing that AMD is benefiting simultaneously from traditional server share gains and the expansion of AI accelerator demand.
The company expects third-quarter revenue of about $13 billion, implying roughly 41% year-over-year growth at the midpoint and around 13% sequential growth. Management also expects Data Center momentum to remain strong in the second half. One increasingly important catalyst is agentic AI. Large-scale inference workloads require more than just GPUs; they also drive demand for CPUs, memory, networking and system-level infrastructure. That gives AMD an opportunity to combine the strength of EPYC with Instinct in a more integrated platform.
High Growth Is Now Confronting High Expectations
After the recent surge, valuation has become the biggest constraint. AMD is trading at roughly 41 times forward 12-month earnings, according to Reuters. While that remains slightly below its 10-year average of around 44 times, the current valuation already assumes sustained high growth in AI-related revenue.
The next phase will therefore depend on execution. Investors will want to see Helios move into meaningful volume deployment, Instinct continue expanding across major customers, and ROCm make further progress in narrowing the software ecosystem gap with CUDA. Competition, fluctuations in hyperscaler capital expenditure, and elevated expectations all suggest that any slowdown in AI order conversion could lead to greater share-price volatility.
Technical Setup: $600 Becomes the Key Level After the Breakout
AMD accelerated from around $493 on September 14 and broke above its prior highs with a gap-up move on September 21. The stock reached an intraday high near $616.7 on heavy volume, putting it into price-discovery territory.
The
$600 level is now the first key support and the main short-term dividing line after the breakout. Below that, the
$582–585 area represents a secondary support zone around the breakout-day low and prior resistance region. A deeper support level sits near
$559–560 . On the upside, the first level to watch is the
$616–620 record-high zone . A clean breakout above that area could open the way toward the $650 psychological level.
Trading Strategy
AMD’s medium-term trend remains strong, but the stock has already moved sharply in a short period, making aggressive chasing above $615 less attractive from a risk-reward perspective. A better setup would be the first controlled pullback toward $600. If the stock tests that area on lighter volume and quickly recovers, the breakout structure would remain intact.
For existing positions, the $582–585 zone can serve as a short-term defensive reference. A sustained break below $580 would suggest weakening momentum, while a further loss of the $559 area would materially damage the current breakout structure.
